doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Playing with Bob Dylan, who changed songs every night
summary: Dylan altered feel, tempo and key nightly, with G.E. Smith, Tony Garnier and Kenny Aaronson adjusting; Parker was with him almost four years.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Okay. Two quick things to wrap up with — every time I read about a review of a Bob Dylan concert they talk about how he plays these tunes different every night. Was that your experience?

Different feel. Different cadences. Different tempos. Different keys. Luckily I was not playing a melodic instrument, but I was with him almost four years and some songs, especially the familiar ones, “Like a Rolling Stone,” “It’s All Over Now,” “Baby Blue,” “Tangled Up in Blue,” “Maggie’s Farm,” “Subterranean Homesick Blues,” things that were more often than not on the set list, at some point in the set list, if Bob thought that we knew what he was going to do he would change it immediately. He didn’t want anybody to phone it in. He didn’t want — he never wanted the feeling, I mean this is my perception — he never wanted anybody to take it for granted that this is the way we’re going to play “Boots of Spanish Leather” because that’s the way we played it last night. We’re going to play it the same way tonight. No, no, no, no. Even something like “The Times They Are A Changin’” which is like a 12/8 kind of lope usually. But if he thought that we were expecting that he would put it in 4/4 or he would put it in — he would change the feel or change the key so that at least bass and guitar had to adjust and get their bearings quickly to keep up.
Well how did he make it known? Did he play something on the guitar to set it up?

Yeah. Or at that time he was playing mostly electric or acoustic guitar and harmonica. Now I understand he plays more keyboard. But at the time I was with him it was always guitar or acoustic guitar. And you would have to watch and listen carefully. Oop, we’re not in G tonight, we’re in B flat. He took it down a step or he took it up a half step you know. Maybe he felt better singing it there or lowered it a half a step to feel better singing. But God bless him you know G.E. Smith, Tony Garnier, or before Tony, Kenny Aaronsson on bass you know, adjusted quickly. All right, here we go. We’re in a different key and we’re in 4/4 on “Times They Are a Changin’” instead of 12/8. But he would rarely make a sound check so we would get sounds for the front of the house guys, the mixer and then Bob would be there for the show. So you never knew what to expect. And there were some, again, cliché, to use the word magical but some really magical moments, especially when he was playing acoustic guitar and harmonica, that thing made you really appreciate what a fantastic iconic artist he is. And the songs themselves, the poetry in the songs is unbelievable. He’s brilliant. Always was. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
